title: A damaged QR code can still tell you what it says
body: A QR code includes **extra mathematical information** that can help a scanner reconstruct damaged data. This technique, called Reed–Solomon error correction, gives the scanner a way to recover missing or incorrect pieces instead of simply guessing. QR codes offer four correction levels, trading extra redundancy for space. Damage can still make a code unreadable, so recovery is never guaranteed.

slides.heading: Built-in repair information
slides.text: The code stores data plus extra information calculated from it. A decoder uses the relationships between those pieces to detect and correct some errors.

left.label: Less correction
left.text: Less space is used for redundancy, leaving more room for the message.

right.label: More correction
right.text: More space goes to repair information, helping the code tolerate more damage.

slides.question: At the highest correction level, out of 10 pieces of a QR code’s data, how many can be lost and still recovered?
slides.explanation: About 3 in 10: level H restores roughly 30% of the codewords, Q 25%, M 15% and L 7%. The more space goes to repair data, the less is left for the message.

slides.heading: Share of a QR code that can be restored, by correction level
slides.note: Approximate share of codewords that can be recovered. Higher levels leave less room for the data.

slides.heading: Why a scratch may be harmless
slides.text: A scratch can destroy some encoded data while leaving enough information to reconstruct it. Too much damage, or trouble locating the code, can still prevent a scan.

slides.question: What is the trade-off of choosing a higher correction level?
slides.explanation: More of the code goes to repair information, so it tolerates more damage but has less space for the data itself. QR codes offer four such levels.

source.label: DENSO WAVE: QR Code Error Correction Feature
